General Ulysses Grant was not known as a vain man, but one thing he prided himself on was his mastery of the English language. And his literary prowess was proved when his memoirs were published and became a best seller. He once told his son, General Frederick Dent Grant, that despite his many victories, his greatest achievement was that in all the orders he wrote in the Civil War, only one was misunderstood. "Son," he said, "the cardinal duty of a commanding officer in war is to be so precise in his use of words that nobody can misconstrue his orders."

The misunderstood order was to General Lew Wallace at the Battle of Shiloh to proceed by the River Road. At the time he wrote the order Grant didn't know that there were two roads locally called the River Road. Wallace took the wrong one. Wallace was court-martialed for it and General grant appeared in his defense. Wallace was acquitted.

This one requires a little more skill to get going because as you can imagine, everything wants to eat it!

Companion plants such as Thai basil (keeps pests away) and celosia argentea (attracts wasps) are important to grow along with amaranth if you want to go organic.

For slugs and other pests it is good to put broken egg shells or even crushed sea shells around the base of the plant.

The plant can grow very tall (6ft+) and is very showy! It produces a wonderfully beautiful flower that catches attention. MANY varieties exist. Some are for grain production, others for seed (seed color also varies from white to black). I made a crossbreed so I get some good leaf production (green to purple) and a good amount of grain.

Once you have seen the little yellow flowers appear, you should wait 2 weeks to harvest. When you see that the seed heads are opening (use a magnifying lens), you can cut the head off. DO NOT uproot the plant as it will produce another smaller flower and then die off.

Once you have harvested the heads, place them in a paper bag with a few holes at the top and let the head dry. The grains should fall to the bottom of the bag when the head is dry. Rub it gently in your hands to get everything out (there will be tons!)

The chaff is easy to get rid of if you simply use a deep dish and blow gently, the chaff will fly away leaving only the seed :)

To store your seeds you need to let them dry on a piece of paper, spread out thin, for about 3 to 4 days (depends on your climate). You will notice that the seeds will shrink considerably, that is your indication that they are ready to go. Place them in an air tight contained with a silica packet or a couple of grains of rice. Store your containers in the freezer (in a thick airtight bag). If done properly your seeds will remain viable (90% germination) for a good 5 or 6 years.

You are obviously not a climate scientist, so you can't possibly comprehend this subject. I'll spell it out for you: climate change/global warming does NOT mean that all weather patterns and phenomenon will get worse and the world will be hotter year round. That's not how climate works, nor is it how physics works. Climate change, which is brought on by global warming, is a disruption in our climate. That means that some places will get far less rain than normal while others get far more rain than normal. Places that usually have no big storms (like hurricanes) might start having more (like in the Pacific) while places that usually have a lot of big storms might have less (like the Atlantic). Just because the end result seems positive in the short term does not mean it will be positive in the long term. It's hard to know exactly how the climate will change in the short term because the overall climate change is interacting with local and global climate systems and their cycles, which are also hard to predict. What we do know for sure is that global warming is taking place at a rate that is far beyond what recent natural cycles have had, and it correlates strongly with human activities. We know that human activities produce things that definitely will promote global warming, so we can infer that human activities are causing the unusual spike in global warming. Even if human activities aren't contributing that much to it, the amount they are might be just enough to break the natural cycle and send things into unnatural territory. Basically what global warming is is trapping in a whole mess of energy that would normally be expelled into space due to thermodynamics. We have more ozone now providing greater insulation, and that's what's trapping in the heat. So, instead of slowly escaping into space at a constant rate over a long period of time, that energy slowly spreads throughout the planet, mostly through the oceans. One or two degrees in ocean temperature might not seem like that much, but when you figure how much energy it took to change the temperature of the ENTIRE OCEAN, it's absolutely insane amounts of energy, and that energy is now affecting our climate patterns both big and small. Imagine you have a cup of cold water and a tub of cold water that are both about 40 degrees F. Obviously the cup can be warmed up rather quickly, but all the water in the tub is going to take a lot more energy to warm up even just a little. Now extrapolate that concept to the entire fucking ocean. Shit loads of energy. Our weather systems get a lot of their energy from the ocean, so if there's more energy in the ocean, we have more energetic weather systems, which means more dynamic changes, not just warmer. Over the long term, however, that energy will slowly dissipate throughout the planet and things will get warmer year round. How long that process takes is anyone's guess, but it could be sooner rather than later.
